context: In fractional knapsack, you can take part of an item and receive the corresponding fraction of its value. The knapsack has capacity 50. Since value equals weight times value per unit of weight, a rectangle whose width is the item's weight and whose height is its unit value has an area equal to the item's value.
description: Five rectangles sit side by side, their heights arranged in nonincreasing order from left to right. The table lists each fruit icon's name, original item number, width, and height. A double-headed arrow below the horizontal axis marks the capacity of 50. It spans the full width of the leftmost rectangle (banana) and extends partway across the second (pineapple).

The diagram labels the widths, heights, and capacity of 50. The table uses those labels to calculate each whole item's value and the weight and value taken. Item numbers match the earlier table. The diagram does not label the total value of 277.5 separately.

frames.explanation: The banana uses 20 of the available 50 units. The remaining 30 cover three quarters of the pineapple's width of 40, leaving 10 units of weight behind. The last three rectangles lie outside the capacity interval. The selected area is 20 × 6 + 30 × 5.25 = 277.5, the maximum total value.
frames.title: A capacity of 50 covers portions of the two rectangles with the highest unit values

summary: Each rectangle's width represents weight, its height represents value per unit of weight, and its area represents value. The rectangles show which items to take first when capacity is limited.

tables.caption: The five items from left to right in the diagram, with value calculated as weight times unit value

title: A geometric view of fractional knapsack
